exp.0:1:
This verse is a greeting. Paul wishes that the believers receive grace, which is the undeserved favor of God, and peace, which is tranquility and reconciliation with God. Both come from God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.

Paul writes together with Silvanus and Timothy to the church in Thessalonica. The believers there were going through persecutions and tribulations. Before encouraging and correcting them, Paul greets them with a wish that sums up what God gives to his people. Placing the Father and Jesus together as the source of grace shows the high place Paul gives to Christ.

For today: when you face pressure or difficulties, remember that grace and peace do not depend on your circumstances, but on God. Ask for them each day, and wish the same for others when you greet them or pray for them.
exp.0:2:
What it says: Paul and his companions say that they must always thank God for the believers in Thessalonica. They do this because it is fitting and right. The reason is that their faith keeps growing, and the love of each one of them for the others abounds.

Context: Paul, Silvanus, and Timothy write to a young church that was suffering persecution. Before they correct or teach about the coming of the Lord, they begin by giving thanks and encouraging them. They recognize that God himself is making these believers grow even in the midst of hardship.

For today: Think of a person in your church or your family whose faith or love has encouraged you. Tell them today, in simple words, that you thank God for their life. Sincere encouragement strengthens someone who is going through trials.
exp.0:3:
Paul says that he and his companions take honest pride in the believers of Thessalonica before other churches. The reason is their patience, which means steady endurance, and their faith in the middle of persecutions and tribulations, that is, attacks and sufferings they kept on living through. Here "boast" is not vanity but thankful joy over what God is doing in them.

Paul writes together with Silas and Timothy to a young church that was under pressure and rejection because of its faith. He has just thanked God because their faith and their love are growing. Now he encourages them by showing that their perseverance is known and admired by other churches. With this he wants to strengthen them to keep going forward.

Today, we can encourage someone who is going through a trial. Tell them sincerely what you see of God in their steadfastness. A word of encouragement can give them strength not to give up.
exp.0:6:
It says that God will give rest to those who suffer for their faith, together with Paul and his companions. That relief will come when the Lord Jesus is revealed, that is, when he appears in full view of everyone, from heaven, accompanied by his mighty angels.

Paul writes together with Silvanus and Timothy to the believers in Thessalonica, who were suffering persecution for following Christ. He wants to encourage them by assuring them that God sees their suffering and is just. The promised rest is tied to the coming of Jesus, and the following verses speak of judgment on those who reject the gospel.

For today: if you are going through a trial because of your faith, you have not been forgotten. You can remain faithful with hope, trusting that God will do justice and give rest in his time, without your having to take revenge yourself.
exp.0:10:
Paul says that he always prays for the Thessalonians. He asks that God would count them worthy of the calling he gave them, and that he would fulfill with power every good desire they have and every work that comes from faith.

Paul writes together with Silas and Timothy to a church that was suffering persecution. He had just spoken about the return of Christ and the judgment. That is why he prays that they will persevere faithfully.

Counting them worthy does not mean that they earn salvation; many understand it to mean living in a way that is consistent with the calling they received.

Today we can pray for other believers, not only that their problems will pass, but that God will strengthen them and help them keep doing good with faith. Choose someone today and pray in this way for that person.
exp.0:11:
It says that Paul and his companions pray that the name of Jesus may be honored through the lives of believers, and that the believers may also be honored in union with him. All of this happens through the grace of God and of Jesus Christ, that is, through his undeserved favor.

Paul writes together with Silvanus and Timothy to a church in Thessalonica that was suffering persecution. In the verses before, he speaks of the day when Christ will come to be glorified in his people. The prayer seeks that they live in a way worthy of their calling, and it reminds them that what they are and what they accomplish comes from grace, not from their own merits.

Today we can ask ourselves each morning: "Lord, how can my work, my dealings with family, and my patience in difficulties honor Jesus?" And we can ask it with humility, trusting that he gives the strength.
exp.1:0:
Paul is making a request of the brothers in Thessalonica, and he begins to speak about two things: the coming of Jesus Christ and our being gathered together to him, that is, the moment when believers will be brought together with Christ. "Now" introduces his request, and "we ask you" conveys that he is appealing to them warmly.

Paul writes together with Silvanus and Timothy to a young church that was confused. Some were saying, even with letters that seemed to come from Paul, that the day of the Lord had already arrived or was very near. This frightened and discouraged them. Paul wants to calm them and correct that mistake.

For today: the hope of Christ's return should give us peace, not fear. Before believing any message about the end of time, let us compare it with what the Bible says, and keep living with faith and steadfastness.
exp.1:1:
Believers should not lose their composure or let their thinking be thrown into confusion. The Berean Standard Bible says they should not be easily disturbed, and that is the idea here: a steady mind that does not panic at every new claim. The word for mind speaks of how we think and reason, so the concern is with a settled, clear-headed outlook.

Some were claiming that the Day of the Lord had already arrived, and they supported this with a supposed prophecy, a spoken message, or a letter that seemed to come from Paul. Paul writes to the church in Thessalonica together with Silvanus and Timothy. The believers were unsettled because false reports about the return of the Lord were reaching them. Paul wants to reassure them and remind them of what he had actually taught them while he was with them.

For today: before believing or repeating an alarming report or prophecy about the end of the age, compare it with what the Bible says. A faith firmly grounded in Scripture gives us peace rather than fear.
exp.1:7:
It says that when the lawless one appears, the man of evil who opposes God, the Lord Jesus will defeat him. The phrase about being consumed by the spirit of his mouth means that his word or his breath will be enough. The brightness of his coming is the shining of his glorious arrival. Being revealed means he will be made known openly.

Paul writes to the Thessalonians, who were frightened because some were saying that the day of the Lord had already arrived. He reminds them that first a great rebellion will come and this figure will be revealed. Who the one who restrains is remains unclear, and Christian interpreters have proposed several ideas. What is certain is that Paul wants to give them calm: Christ has the final victory.

For today: when evil seems to be advancing and fear troubles you, remember that Jesus has the last word. Stand firm in the truth, love it, and trust in him.
exp.2:3:
Paul tells the believers in Thessalonica that he is confident in them. That confidence does not rest only on them, but in the Lord. He believes they are already doing what he has commanded and that they will continue to do so.

Paul writes together with Silvanus and Timothy to a church facing opposition. He has just asked for prayers and reminded them that the Lord is faithful. Now he encourages them with confidence before correcting those who were living in disorder and refusing to work. His encouragement prepares the ground for a firm correction. The word "command" here means instructions given with authority.

For today: let us encourage others with sincere confidence, and not only with scolding. When someone guides us in the faith, we can respond with humble obedience, relying on the fact that God is the one who sustains us. Today, encourage someone by reminding them of what they already do well in the Lord.
exp.2:4:
Paul prays that the Lord will "direct" the hearts of the Thessalonians, that is, that he will guide them and put them on the right course. That course has two parts: the love of God, which can be understood as the love God has for us or the love we give to him, and the patient waiting for Christ, which can be the steadfastness Christ showed or the steadfastness he gives us to wait for him.

Paul writes together with Silvanus and Timothy to a church that was under pressure and confused about the Lord's coming. He has just expressed confidence in them, and now he entrusts them to God, before correcting those who were living in a disorderly way.

For today: when life wears you out or pressures you, ask God to orient your heart toward his love and give you endurance, instead of depending only on your own strength.
exp.2:6:
Paul reminds the Thessalonians that they already know how they ought to follow his example. To follow an example means to copy the way of life that he and his companions showed them. Paul says that he and his companions did not live without discipline or responsibility when they were with them.

Paul writes together with Silas and Timothy. Earlier, he had instructed them to keep away from the brothers who were living in an undisciplined way, that is, those who would not work and depended on others. To correct them, he does not give only a command; he reminds them of the example they themselves saw. What follows explains that they worked hard so as not to be a burden to anyone.

For today: strive to make your life consistent with what you say you believe. Be responsible in your work, in your debts, and in your commitments, so that others can see in you a simple and trustworthy example of faith.
exp.2:12:
This verse encourages believers not to give up or become worn out in doing good. "Do not grow weary" means not to lose heart or let go.

Paul writes, together with Silvanus and Timothy, to the church in Thessalonica. Some of the brothers were living without working and were meddling in other people's affairs. Paul corrects them firmly, but now he speaks to those who are doing what is right, so that the bad conduct of a few does not lead them to grow weary of helping. The verses that follow call for correction to be given with love, as to a brother.

Today, if you serve in your church or help someone and you feel tired or undervalued, remember that doing good does not lose its worth. Ask God for strength, rest when you need to, and keep doing what is good with wisdom and patience.
exp.2:16:
Paul says that this greeting is written in his own hand, and that this is his mark in all his letters. "Greeting" here means the greeting itself. A "mark" is a personal sign or signature. It is like signing a letter at the end, to show it is genuinely his.

Paul used to dictate his letters to an assistant, and at the end he would add a few lines in his own handwriting. Here he does this to give the letter authenticity, perhaps because a false letter in his name was circulating in Thessalonica (2:2). Many scholars read it this way. The closing note about Athens is not part of the original inspired text, and its accuracy is debated.

Today we can make sure that what we hear as coming from God is faithful to his Word. Before believing any message, let us compare it with the Bible. And may our own word be trustworthy, like a signature that stands behind what we say.
exp.2:17:
Paul closes the letter by wishing that the grace of Jesus Christ, that is, his undeserved favor and kindness, be with all the believers in Thessalonica.

Paul writes to a young church that was facing persecution and confusion about the coming of Christ. He had just said he was signing with his own hand so that they would know the letter was genuine. His farewell reflects pastoral affection: he wants everyone, without leaving anyone out, to receive God's grace. The closing note says the letter was written from Athens; that note is not part of Paul's original text. Copyists added it later, and today many scholars doubt that it is correct.

For today: do not live your faith as a burden of merits. Begin and end the day asking for the grace of Jesus, and wish it also for those around you, even for the people who are hard to get along with.
exp.1:4:
Paul asks them a question with affection, but also with a gentle rebuke: "Do you not remember?" He reminds them that while he was still with them in Thessalonica, he had already taught them these things about the man of lawlessness and the rebellion. The word for the rebellion means abandoning the faith.

Paul writes to a young church that was confused and frightened. Some were saying that the day of the Lord had already arrived. Paul reminds them of what they had already learned, so that they would not be deceived. Scholars interpret in various ways who the "man of lawlessness" is, and the Bible does not give a name here.

For today: do not be carried away by rumors or by fears. Return again and again to what God's Word already teaches, and remember it. A firm faith rests on the truth you have learned, not on every piece of news you hear.
exp.1:9:
It says that the lawless one, the "man of sin," comes with every kind of wicked deception directed against those who are perishing. These deceptions trap them because they refused the love of the truth, that is, they did not welcome it or want it, and so they were not saved. Those who are perishing are those on the way to eternal ruin.

Paul writes to the believers in Thessalonica, who were frightened and confused about the return of Christ. He explains that first a great rebellion will come, and a lawless one who will act with false signs. People interpret this in different ways, but Paul wants his readers to be firm and not to be deceived.

Today, the best defense against deception is not only knowing more, but loving the truth. Read the Bible with a heart willing to obey it, even when it is uncomfortable, and ask God to keep you firm.
exp.2:10:
Paul says he has heard that some of you are leading undisciplined lives, accomplishing nothing, and are busy being busybodies, meddling in other people's affairs and spreading gossip.

Paul, together with Silvanus and Timothy, writes to a young church. He had already set an example by working with his own hands so as not to be a burden to anyone. Some interpret this idleness as coming from expecting Christ to return soon, but the text does not state this clearly. What it does ask is that they work quietly and earn their own bread.

Today we can ask ourselves how we spend our time. Instead of giving opinions about the lives of others, let us take up our own tasks responsibly, serving with steadiness and without complaint.
exp.2:8:
Paul says that he and his companions had the right to receive support from the Thessalonians, but they did not claim it. They chose to do this to give them an example, so that they could imitate them. Paul's right to support is what the verse refers to when it speaks of a "right," meaning the entitlement to claim it.

Paul writes to the church in Thessalonica, together with Silvanus and Timothy. Some in the community were living without working and were meddling in other people's affairs. Paul reminds them that he worked night and day so as not to be a burden to anyone. His life backed up what he taught: whoever does not want to work should not eat either.

For today: try to make your way of living a good example, especially in your work and responsibilities. Honestly carry out what is yours to do, without taking advantage of others. Sometimes we teach more by what we do than by what we say.
exp.1:2:
Paul warns the believers not to be deceived in any way. He says the day of the Lord will not come until the rebellion takes place and the man of lawlessness is revealed, called the son of destruction, someone destined for ruin.

Paul writes to the church in Thessalonica. Some believed, perhaps because of a rumor or a forged letter, that the day of the Lord had already come or was very near, and this troubled them. Paul wants to give them calm. Who the "man of lawlessness" is has been interpreted in several ways, and the Bible does not give a name here.

For today: before believing any alarming news or prediction, check it against the Bible. Keep calm, stand firm in Christ, and live faithfully.
exp.2:5:
Paul gives a serious command to the believers in Thessalonica. He says, "we command you," and he gives this command in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. They are to keep away from every brother who leads an undisciplined life, one that is not in keeping with the teaching they received from the apostles.

Paul, together with Silvanus and Timothy, writes to a young church. According to the verses that follow, the problem was that some did not want to work and lived off others. Paul reminds them that he himself worked hard so as not to be a burden. Many understand this "keep away" as keeping a loving distance in order to correct, not to hate.

For today: if a brother lives in a way that harms others, we should not ignore it or help him continue the same way. Let us speak with kindness and truth, and let us live ourselves with responsibility and a good witness.
exp.1:15:
Here the verse says that Jesus Christ and God the Father have loved us and given us eternal comfort and good hope. All of this is "by grace," that is, as a gift we do not deserve. The word "comfort" here means encouragement in the middle of difficulty.

Paul writes to the Christians of Thessalonica, together with his companions. They were going through pressure and were confused about the return of Christ. Before this verse, Paul encouraged them to stand firm in what they had been taught. Here he shifts to a prayer of blessing: he asks that our Lord Jesus Christ and God our Father would strengthen them, because their steadfastness depends on his love.

For today: when you feel tired or afraid of the future, remember first that God has already loved you and given you hope. Before you strain to endure, take a moment to pray, thanking him for that comfort, and ask him to sustain your heart.
exp.2:1:
Paul asks the Thessalonians to pray that he and his companions will be rescued from wicked and evil men. The word "evil" here refers to people who are troublesome, dishonest, or harmful, who get in the way and do damage. Then he explains: "for not everyone holds to the faith," meaning not everyone believes, and that is why some oppose the gospel.

Paul writes together with Silvanus and Timothy to a young church. He asks for prayer so that the word of the Lord may spread freely while he faces opposition. According to Acts, in cities such as Corinth, where he was probably staying when he wrote, his message met resistance. Right after this, he reminds them that the Lord is faithful and will guard them from the evil one.

For today: pray for those who preach and serve in your church, and do not lose heart when others reject your faith. Trust that God is faithful and will sustain you.
exp.2:15:
The passage says that the Lord himself, the one who is the source of peace, would give them peace at all times and in every way. It ends with a blessing: that the Lord be with all of them. The words "to you" in the verse are the English equivalent of this line, and "all of you" refers to everyone in the group being addressed.

Paul is writing to the Christians in Thessalonica. He has just asked them to correct, with love, anyone who does not follow his instructions, without treating that person as an enemy. There were tensions in the church, and that is why his wish for peace comes right after.

For today: when there are conflicts in your family or your church, ask God for his peace before you react. Correct others with humility, and treat the other person as a brother or sister, not as a rival.
exp.1:5:
The Thessalonians already knew what is restraining the "lawless one." "Restraining" means that it holds him back. "At the proper time" means that he will be revealed only at the appointed moment, and not before.

Paul writes to a frightened church, since some were saying that the day of the Lord had already arrived. He reminds them of what he taught them in person. But we do not know what it is that is "restraining"; Paul does not say it here. It has been understood as human government, the Roman Empire, civil order, the work of the Spirit, or an angelic power. No view is certain.

For today: you do not need to figure out every detail to live in peace. God is in control of the times, even of evil. Trust him, stand firm in the truth, and do not let rumors or predictions frighten you.
exp.2:14:
It tells us not to treat as an enemy someone who does not obey, but to correct him with affection, as a brother. "Admonish" means to warn and advise so that someone will change. The words "do not regard him as an enemy" and "as a brother" are the wording the verse itself uses, so they need no further comment.

Paul writes to the church in Thessalonica. Some were living without working and were disobeying his instructions. Paul asks that the church keep away from them so that they will feel shame and respond. But he makes clear that this distance is not rejection or hatred. His goal is that the brother return to the good path and to fellowship.

When someone in the church or in the family makes a mistake, avoid speaking badly of him or treating him with contempt. Speak to him with truth and tenderness, seeking his good. Correcting with love shows that we still consider him part of God's family.
exp.0:9:
This verse speaks of the day when Jesus returns. It says that Christ will be glorified in his saints, that is, in his people, and that he will be regarded with wonder by all who have believed. Here "regarded with wonder" means that he will cause amazement and worship. The words about the Thessalonians themselves make clear that they are included, because they believed the testimony of Paul and his companions.

Paul writes, together with Silvanus and Timothy, to a church that was suffering persecution. The verses before this one speak of God's justice against those who reject the gospel. This verse shifts the focus: for believers, that day will be one of glory, not fear. Paul wants to encourage them to endure, reminding them that their suffering is not the end of the story.

For today: when you feel tired or overlooked for following Christ, remember that your faith is not in vain. Live today with the hope of that day, and let that hope give you patience and steadiness.
exp.1:11:
What it says: Paul explains that those who did not believe the truth of the gospel, and instead took delight in wickedness, will face judgment. "Judgment" here means a sentence that carries punishment. "Wickedness" means injustice or sin. To "delight in" something means they gave their agreement to it and found pleasure in it.

Context: Paul writes to the Christians in Thessalonica, who were frightened and confused about the day of the Lord. He tells them that a strong deception will come before that day. He points out that the problem of those who were deceived was not a lack of information, but that they refused to love the truth. Then Paul encourages the believers: God chose them for salvation.

For today: Examine what things you enjoy and what you give your approval to. Ask God to give you a love for his truth, and read it every day so you are not carried away by what sounds good but is false.
exp.2:2:
This verse says that the Lord always keeps what he promises. He will strengthen believers and guard them from the evil one. The word "strengthen" means to make firm or secure, and "guard" means to protect. Because the verse speaks of "the evil one," it points to a personal source of harm, and the rest of the verse's wording gives the reader a clear picture of the Lord's care.

Paul is writing to the Christians in Thessalonica. He has just asked them to pray for him because he faces people who are troublesome and wicked, that is, annoying and perverse people who opposed the gospel. Noticing that not everyone believes, he moves from his need to confidence: even when people fail, the Lord is faithful.

For today: when you feel pressure, fear, or rejection because of your faith, do not rely only on your own strength. Ask the Lord to sustain you, and remember that his faithfulness does not depend on circumstances. Pray also for other believers who are going through trials.
exp.0:5:
Paul says that it is only right for God to repay with affliction those who afflict the believers. To "repay" means to give back the consequence that is deserved, and to "afflict" means to cause distress, pressure, or persecution. God does not overlook injustice.

Paul writes, together with Silvanus and Timothy, to the Christians of Thessalonica, who were suffering persecution for their faith. He wants to encourage them: their perseverance shows that God is just, and in the end He will set everything right. The verses that follow speak of rest for them when Jesus returns.

For today: if people treat you badly because of your faith, do not take revenge. Trust that God sees everything and judges with perfect justice. In the meantime, keep loving, pray for those who harm you, and stand firm.
exp.1:3:
He says this "man of sin" sets himself against God and rises up against every so-called god or object of worship. He goes so far as to take a seat in the temple of God, proclaiming himself to be God.

Paul writes to the believers in Thessalonica, who were frightened because someone was saying that the day of the Lord had already arrived. He makes clear to them that first there will come a rebellion against God and the appearance of this opponent. Christians interpret in different ways whether the temple is literal or symbolic, and who this figure is.

For today: do not let yourself be shaken by rumors or fears about the end. Test what you hear against the Bible, and keep your heart steady, worshiping God alone, and giving no thing and no person his place.
exp.0:8:
Paul says that those who reject God and do not obey the gospel will receive a punishment of eternal ruin, separated from the presence of the Lord and the glory of His might. The word "might" translates the term for strength or power in the original. The phrase "separated from the presence of the Lord" can be understood as "far from his presence," and that is how some readers understand it. Christians understand in different ways what that ruin consists of.

Paul, together with Silvanus and Timothy, writes to the believers in Thessalonica, who were suffering persecution. He wants to comfort them: God is just, he will see their suffering, and when Jesus returns he will set everything right.

Today, if people mistreat you because of your faith, you do not have to take revenge. You can trust that God will judge with justice. And since the punishment is real and serious, this text also encourages you to share the gospel with love and to pray for those who do not yet know Jesus.
exp.2:13:
Paul says that if anyone does not obey what he has written in this letter, the church should take note of that person. The church should also stop associating with that person, so that they feel shame and reflect on their conduct. The Greek words here carry the sense of drawing close to someone, so this means avoiding close dealings with them.

Paul writes to the believers in Thessalonica. Some were living without working and were causing disorder, even though they had already been urged to work quietly. Paul asks that the church support his teaching. The verses that follow make clear that this is not rejection: the person is not treated as an enemy, but as a brother to be admonished.

When someone in the church persists in a clear error, we may keep our distance with humility and firmness, but without hostility. The goal is their restoration, so we continue praying for that person and speaking to them with kindness and truth.
exp.0:4:
This verse says that the suffering of the Thessalonians is a sign or proof that God judges justly. God will count them worthy of his kingdom, the same kingdom for which they now suffer. Being counted worthy does not mean they earn their salvation; it means God will recognize that their faith is real. The word "clear evidence" here means sign or proof. Some understand the sign to be the strength God gives them; others, that it points to the future judgment.

Paul writes, together with Silvanus and Timothy, to a young church that was suffering persecution. First he thanks them for their faith and their growing love. Then he encourages them, saying that God does not overlook their pain, and that he will do justice when Christ returns.

Today, if you suffer for following Christ, your pain is not in vain. God sees it and uses it. Trust in his justice, keep on loving, and ask him to strengthen your faith.
exp.1:12:
Paul says that he should always thank God for the believers in Thessalonica, whom he calls brothers who are loved by the Lord. He reminds them that God chose them from the beginning to be saved. Here, being saved means being rescued from sin and its consequences. This happens through the work of the Spirit, who makes them holy, that is, set apart for God, and through faith in the truth.

Paul writes together with Silas and Timothy. He has just spoken about those who reject the truth and will be condemned. Now he contrasts the Thessalonians with them, to give them security and encouragement in the face of confusion and persecution. Christians debate how to understand election: some see it as God's decision about specific people, others as his plan for those who believe.

For today: if you trust in Christ, your salvation rests on the work of God, not on your own strength. Respond with gratitude and keep growing in the truth.
exp.2:11:
In this verse, Paul and his companions firmly ask, in the name of Jesus Christ, that certain people begin working quietly and earn their own living. The word translated "command" means to ask with authority, and the word translated "urge" means to ask with affection. "Quietly" here means in an orderly and calm way, and "such people" refers to those who were living in disorder.

Paul writes to the church in Thessalonica. Some were not working but were interfering in other people's lives, and they lived at the expense of others. Some think they had stopped working because they were expecting Christ to return, but the text does not say this clearly. Paul gives a serious call, yet he also speaks to them as brothers.

For today: do your work with responsibility and peace, without depending on others out of laziness, and be careful not to meddle in matters that are not your concern. Help with love those who truly need it.
exp.1:6:
Paul says that lawlessness is already at work in secret in the world. "Mystery of lawlessness" refers to a hidden wickedness that is not yet fully seen. The phrase "the one who now restrains it" means that someone or something is holding it back for now, but only until that restraint is "taken out of the way," that is, removed.

Paul writes to the Thessalonians, who were confused and frightened, thinking the day of the Lord had already arrived. He reminds them of what he had taught them in person. Before that day the lawless one will come, and the Lord will overcome him. Who it is that restrains is not known for certain; Christian interpreters have proposed several answers.

Today we can live with calm and alertness. Evil is active, but Christ has the final victory. For that reason we should remain firm in the truth, pray, and not allow ourselves to be deceived by fear or by false news.
exp.1:16:
It says that God himself, our Lord Jesus Christ and God the Father, is the one who can encourage and comfort our hearts. He can also strengthen us to stand firm in every good word and deed. The word "encourage" here is a prayer or wish: "may he encourage." The word "strengthen" means to make firm and steady.

Paul writes to the Christians of Thessalonica, together with Silas and Timothy. Some were frightened and confused by false reports about the return of Christ. Paul asks them to stay firm in the teaching they received, and now he prays that God himself would uphold them. He not only gives them a command, he also pleads for them.

For today: when you feel unsure or tired, ask God for encouragement and strength. Then take one concrete step: say a kind word or do a good deed today.
exp.0:0:
Paul writes this letter together with Silvanus and Timothy, addressed to the church of the Thessalonians. The letter is sent to this church, and the wording used for the church describes people who live joined to God our Father and to the Lord Jesus Christ.

Paul is the one who leads the letter, and he adds the names of his fellow workers, who had been with him when that church was founded (Acts 17). He writes to believers who are young in the faith and who faced pressure and suffering. Many think this letter was written shortly after the first one, although the exact date is not known for certain.

For today: our firmest identity is not the place where we live or what happens to us, but being "in God" and "in Christ." When difficulties come, remember that you belong to Him, and seek support in your community of faith.
exp.0:7:
This verse says that Jesus will come from heaven "in blazing fire" and will bring just repayment on those who do not know God and do not obey the gospel of our Lord Jesus. "Inflicting vengeance" here means bringing repayment or justice. "Know God" refers to knowing Him truly, not merely knowing about Him. The "blazing fire" is an image of his holiness and judgment, and scholars understand it in different ways: literally or symbolically.

Paul writes to the believers in Thessalonica, who were suffering persecution for their faith. He wants to encourage them by reminding them that God sees their suffering and that in the end he will do justice. Judgment does not rest in human hands, but in those of Christ, when he returns.

For today: if you suffer for following Jesus or because of injustice, you can rest in the knowledge that God will bring justice in his time. So do not seek revenge; instead, pray for those who harm you, and keep obeying the gospel with patience and hope.
exp.1:8:
The one called "the lawless one" (also known as "the man of sin") will arrive through the working of Satan. He will come with every kind of power, with signs and false wonders, miracles meant to deceive. "Coming" means arrival, and "working" means action or activity.

Paul writes to the Christians of Thessalonica, who were troubled because they thought the day of the Lord had already arrived. He explains to them that first there will be a great rebellion and that this figure will appear. Christians have understood in different ways who he is and when he will appear, but all agree that Christ will overcome him.

For today: do not be swayed only by what is miraculous or spectacular. Test everything against the Word of God, love the truth, and stand firm in Christ, who holds the final victory.
exp.1:13:
He says that God called the believers of Thessalonica through the gospel that Paul preached to them. This calling has a goal: that they share in the glory of Jesus Christ. Here "share in" means taking part in something God gives.

Paul writes to a young church that was confused by false teachings about the Lord's return. He has just spoken of those who reject the truth and will be condemned. Now he contrasts that with the believers: they were called by God and have a future of glory. He wants to give them assurance and encouragement.

For today: if you have put your faith in Christ, your life has a secure destination. When doubts or fear come, remember that God called you and He will finish His work. Respond with gratitude and steadfastness.
exp.2:0:
Paul asks the believers in Thessalonica to keep praying for him and his companions. "Finally" here means "at last" or "moreover." He wants the message of the Lord to spread quickly, without hindrance, and to be held in honor and well received, just as it was among them.

The apostle Paul writes here together with Silvanus and Timothy, as the greeting of the letter shows. He writes to a young church that had received the gospel well. Paul himself faced opposition, and that is why he asks for prayer, as the next verse makes clear.

Today we can pray regularly for those who preach and share the gospel, including missionaries and pastors. Ask that God open doors, give courage, and touch hearts. You can also ask that your own life bring honor to the word of God.
exp.1:14:
Paul tells the believers in Thessalonica to stand firm and to cling to what they were taught. The word "cling" means to hold on tightly. The teachings here are the instruction they received, both what they heard spoken and what they read in a letter.

Paul writes, together with Silas and Timothy, to a young and confused church. Some were saying that the day of the Lord had already come, and this troubled them. Before this verse, Paul reminds them that God chose them and called them through the gospel. Because of this, he now encourages them not to be swayed by rumors.

For today: do not let yourself be carried along by every new opinion you hear. Return often to the Bible, compare what you hear with it, and ask God to keep you firm.
exp.2:7:
Paul says that he and his companions did not eat anyone's food without paying for it. Instead, they worked hard, with labor and toil, night and day, so that they would not be a burden to any of the believers. The next verse calls Paul's conduct an example, meaning a model or pattern for others to follow.

Paul is writing to the believers in Thessalonica. Some of them were living in disorder: they were living without working and depending on others. Paul reminds them of his own example. He had the right to receive support for his ministry, but he chose to work so that he could show them how to live with responsibility.

For today: try to be someone who contributes and is not a burden. Work honestly with what is within your reach, and if you need help today, receive it with gratitude and look for a way to get back on your feet again.
exp.2:9:
Paul is recalling a rule he had already given them in person: if anyone is unwilling to work, he shall not eat. The phrase "gave you this command" points to a firm order or warning. The rule speaks not of someone who cannot work, but of someone who is unwilling to.

Paul writes together with Silvanus and Timothy to the church in Thessalonica. They had worked day and night so as not to be a burden to anyone, even though they had the right to receive support. Now they hear that some are living without working, meddling in the affairs of others. Paul seeks to correct them with love and order.

For today: do your work responsibly and do not live at the expense of others when you are able to support yourself. At the same time, help generously those who truly cannot provide for themselves.
exp.1:10:
He says that God allows certain people to fall under a powerful delusion, so that they end up believing the lie. The verse in the source calls this a force that leads into deception. The word "therefore" shows that this is a consequence of what came before: they rejected the truth, and so the deception catches up with them.

Paul is writing to the believers in Thessalonica, who were frightened by false teachings about the return of Christ. He speaks of the lawless one, a figure of rebellion who deceives with false signs. Those who are lost are the ones who did not receive the love of the truth. Right after this, Paul gives thanks because the Thessalonians were chosen and did believe the truth. Interpreters debate how God acts here, whether he hands people over or hardens them.

Today: loving the truth means caring for the heart. Read the Bible with humility, accept correction, and do not hold only to what pleases you to hear.

sum.0: Paul, Silvanus, and Timothy give thanks to God because the faith and love of the Thessalonians keep growing, even in the middle of persecution. They remind them that God is just: he will give rest to those who are suffering, and he will punish those who reject the gospel when Jesus is revealed. For this reason they pray that God will make them worthy of his calling and that Christ will be glorified in them.
sum.2: Paul asks the Thessalonians to pray for him and for the message of the Lord, and he reminds them that God is faithful and will protect them from the evil one. He tells them to keep away from anyone who lives in a disorderly way and refuses to work, since he himself set an example by working. He asks them to correct such people with love, as brothers and sisters, and not to grow tired of doing good.
sum.1: Paul asks the Thessalonians not to be deceived into thinking that the day of the Lord has already arrived, since first there will be a great rebellion and the appearance of the "man of lawlessness," whom Jesus will destroy when he comes. He encourages them to give thanks for their salvation, to stand firm in what they have been taught, and to trust in the comfort of God.
